- The first experiment successfully established a baseline kinetic profile. As expected for a single standard condition, many models can fit the data equally well by adjusting their rate constants, leading to very similar NLL values (ranging from -20.3 to -17.5).
- My aim for the first turn was achieved. The next step is to perturb the system to break this degeneracy and separate the models based on their specific mechanistic features.

<hypothesis>
- **Hypothesis discrimination**: The leading models include mechanisms with substrate inhibition/deactivation (M7, M11, M16), product deactivation (M12, M17), and standard or higher-order catalyst mechanisms (M1, M2). The most useful feature to test next is whether the system is sensitive to product-induced deactivation.
- **Discriminative experiment design**: I propose an experiment with a high initial product concentration ([P]0 = 0.5), while keeping the substrate and catalyst concentrations identical to the baseline ([S]0 = 1.0, [cat]0 = 0.05). This directly isolates the effect of the product on the reaction kinetics.
- **Contrastive prediction**:
  - For M12 (`P+cat=>inactive`) and M17 (`P+catS=>inactive`), the high initial concentration of P will cause immediate and rapid deactivation of the catalyst from t=0. This will manifest as a severely reduced initial rate and a much lower final conversion compared to the baseline experiment.
  - For M11 (`S+cat=>inactive`) and M16 (`S+catS=>inactive`), the initial rate and deactivation profile will be largely unaffected by the presence of initial P, resulting in a conversion profile very similar to the baseline.
  - For M1 and M7, there is no irreversible deactivation by P. The reaction will proceed to full conversion (or standard equilibrium), clearly distinguishing them from the product-deactivation models.
</hypothesis>
